title: Things to do in New Orleans: 5 places by neighbourhood
description: Explore five places in New Orleans: Jackson Square, French Market, the WWII Museum, City Park and Audubon Park, with neighbourhood routes and practical advice.
keyword: things to do in New Orleans
relatedQueries: places to visit in New Orleans
intro: A first visit to New Orleans can combine five places offering different experiences: Jackson Square, French Market, the National WWII Museum, City Park and Audubon Park. The first two belong to the French Quarter, the museum is in the Arts & Warehouse District, and the parks require other outings. Grouping them by neighbourhood helps you build a meaningful day with time to eat, look around and rest.

This selection combines cultural interpretation and green spaces for different interests. Entering every attraction is unnecessary: choose a museum with substantial content, a market walk or a spacious park according to your available time. The photographs document the places on earlier dates. They do not establish a current exhibition, weather conditions or whether every individual business will be trading during your trip.

sections.heading: 1. Jackson Square: find your bearings in the French Quarter
paragraphs: Jackson Square is a historic garden of approximately two and a half acres, bordered by Chartres, St. Ann, Decatur and St. Peter streets. The municipality places it in the heart of the French Quarter overlooking the Mississippi River area. It provides a useful setting for observing the relationship between gardens, Saint Louis Cathedral and neighbouring buildings. Walk around before continuing through the district, allowing the stop to be more than one photograph of the church façade.

Distinguish the enclosed garden from the streets and pedestrian spaces around it. The city publishes garden opening times, with an earlier winter closure; walking around the neighbourhood does not mean the park itself is accessible at any hour. The photograph shows the square’s setting and cathedral, but entering the church would involve separate conditions. If you encounter an activity or temporary installation, follow the signs and keep access clear. A space available on one day may have another use on the next visit.

sections.heading: 2. French Market: choose between stalls and businesses
paragraphs: French Market lets you continue through the lower French Quarter without repeatedly changing areas. It brings together market stalls, shops and places to eat. Avoid treating it as one business with identical operations across every space. Decide which part interests you first: you can focus on browsing stalls, finding a particular item or taking a meal break without feeling obliged to buy something at each stop.

For an object, ask about origin and authorship if those matter to you; for food, compare the displayed menu and price before ordering. The operator lists vendors seven days a week, including holidays, while allowing certain retailers and eateries to decide their own opening days. Its visitor page also gives different hours in the main text and footer. Avoid arranging a late-afternoon arrival around only one of those times. Check the particular stall or business you want to visit.

sections.heading: 3. National WWII Museum: give the interpretation enough time
paragraphs: The National WWII Museum is in the Arts & Warehouse District and explores the American experience of the Second World War through objects, personal accounts and interpretive resources. This is a substantial thematic visit rather than a general exhibition about New Orleans history. Choose galleries according to your interests and allow time to read. Giving it only whatever remains between two other walks can leave little opportunity to engage with its content.

General admission is different from the Beyond All Boundaries and Priddy Family Freedom Theater experiences. The operator explains what each product covers and recommends advance purchase, while also allowing onsite ticket sales. Check the combination before paying and avoid assuming a special reservation includes the entire campus. The visitor entrance identified by the museum is at 525 Andrew Higgins Boulevard. The address of a parking garage or associated building should not replace that reference when arranging your arrival.

sections.heading: 4. City Park: decide on a section before arriving
paragraphs: City Park combines green spaces and activities across approximately 1,300 acres. Start with a manageable area and a purpose: walking among trees, looking at the water, finding somewhere to pause or entering a particular attraction. The operator describes free and ticketed activities, alongside lakes and walking trails. Its size makes arriving with a plan to explore absolutely everything after an already full day an impractical approach.

For a first walk, locate the access point for your selected area and the place from which you will return. The photograph of bridges and vegetation depicts one part of City Park, not a promise that the entire site has the same appearance. Gardens, facilities and activities can have separate tickets, closures and terms. With children or people who prefer shorter distances, choose a comfortable section and a break. The extent of the park need not become an obligation to walk further.

sections.heading: 5. Audubon Park: live oaks and a walk in Uptown
paragraphs: Audubon Park is in Uptown and offers another urban park setting, with live oaks, a lagoon and an exercise route described by the operator as 1.8 miles long. It is different from City Park. If tree-filled landscapes appeal to you, it can be your main green-space outing rather than an extra stop added without time to stay in either park. Select part of the walk and observe how shade, water and paths work together.

The National Park Service record gives context about John Charles Olmsted’s design, begun in 1898, and identifies Audubon Nature Institute as the manager. That historical information page does not establish federal park ownership or a combined admission pass. Also distinguish a park walk from the zoo and facilities with their own conditions. The operator lists the address as 6500 Magazine Street; use its map to identify the entrance that suits the section you intend to explore.

sections.heading: Opening times, holidays and separate admissions
paragraphs: The museum lists 9am–5pm opening and closures on Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and Mardi Gras Day. Review its calendar before dedicating an outing to one of those dates. It also explains that it is a private nonprofit institution and national park passes are not valid for admission. If frequent rests are important, consult its accessibility information: the campus is large, and individual gallery arrangements matter more than an assumed visit duration.

For open spaces, Jackson Square’s municipal information distinguishes the garden, with 8am–6pm winter hours, from the surrounding urban area. Audubon Park lists daily opening from 5am to 10pm. These are consulted references and remain subject to changes; follow local notices. In City Park, separating public space from ticketed attractions avoids assuming everything is free or every building follows one timetable. French Market requires checking the particular business because of the inconsistent hours published on its own visitor page.

sections.heading: Connect neighbourhoods and choose a convenient base
paragraphs: Jackson Square and French Market form a compact French Quarter outing. The museum involves another walking or transport leg, while City Park and Audubon Park are in other sections of the city and deserve separate planning. RTA provides a trip planner, system map and service alerts, alongside fare information and Le Pass payment guidance. Consult those tools for your travel date, choosing the correct stop and a workable return. A transport ticket is different from museum admission.

When comparing accommodation, establish its actual entrance and the connections to your preferred activities. Time to return for a rest can be more valuable than trying to stay equally close to all five places. Bring water and sun or rain protection according to the forecast; an archive photograph is not a weather report. The Washington, New York and Miami guides linked below help compare other United States travel stages without implying that those cities are nearby excursions from New Orleans.

itinerary: First route: explore Jackson Square, then continue towards French Market with a meal break. If entering the National WWII Museum on the same day, limit the earlier walk enough to retain a substantial museum block and transfer time. You can also give the museum its own outing.

Park route: choose City Park or Audubon Park according to your interests and accommodation. Establish an entrance area, your intended activity and the journey back. That is often more comfortable than crossing the city to check off both parks in one short period.

With longer available, separate the museum, French Quarter and parks into different blocks. Rearrange around holiday closures or rain after confirming that your alternative is open too. Do not assume a paid attraction is included simply because it stands within a park.

faq.question: What should I see on a first trip to New Orleans?
faq.answer: This selection includes Jackson Square, French Market, the National WWII Museum, City Park and Audubon Park. Group the first two and give the museum and green-space outings other blocks of time.

faq.question: Can I walk between all five places?
faq.answer: They should not be treated as one continuous walk. Jackson Square and French Market share an area; the museum and parks require checking distances and connections from your starting point.

faq.question: Does a national park pass include the WWII Museum?
faq.answer: No. The museum explicitly states that it is outside the National Park System and those passes are not valid for admission. Compare general entry and additional experiences separately.

faq.question: Must I visit both City Park and Audubon Park?
faq.answer: That is optional. Each offers green space in a different location with different characteristics. Choose one if time is limited, and visit both when you can allow a comfortable outing for each.

conclusion: New Orleans can combine a walkable district, a museum with substantial interpretation and spacious parks without filling every hour. Choose the interiors that interest you and the green space that fits your pace. Grouping the five places by area leaves time to appreciate what brought you to the city.
